Classical research on political behavior emphasizes that education, internal efficacy, political interest, political knowledge, and participation are central to democratic engagement [17–19]. These factors are often normatively valued because they help citizens follow politics and take part in democratic life. Yet even classical theories recognized that engagement could become excessive [20], and more recent work on motivated reasoning and political polarization suggests that politically engaged citizens may also be more likely to process information in biased or antagonistic ways [21]. To obtain our data, we commissioned the survey agency YouGov to invite panelists from their standing web panel to participate in a series of panel surveys. We recruited the original set of panelists in January 2019. Here, participants were asked to complete a survey with measures of our set of potential antecedents of online political hostility and, importantly, to provide their X ID and give consent to let us scrape their publicly available X data and link it to their survey answers.", "page": 5}]}, {"claim": "The primary measure of online political hostility is validated through multiple methods including face validity, convergent and discriminant validity, criterion validity, external validity, and ecological validity.", "quotes": [{"text": "The SU approach was also validated against 2,469 hand-labeled posts rated by four expert raters using the definition of \"Political Hostility\" as: \"Degrading, harassing and intimidating online content grounded in political differences.\" [60]. The expert-coded set was approximately balanced across the two classes, so a naive baseline (always predicting the majority class) would achieve about 0.50 accuracy. We trained the score on a training split of these labelled posts and evaluated it on a held-out test split from the same domain (i.e., panelist posts), thereby avoiding in-sample inflation.
